analysis.headline: Introduced February 14, 2023 with 9 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats; referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote, markup, or hearing before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: A stock buyback is when a company buys back its own shares on the open market, which returns cash to shareholders instead of spending it on wages, factories, or research. Since 2023, a 1% federal excise tax has applied to those repurchases. This bill would have quadrupled that tax to 4%, and would also have stopped companies from reducing the tax by counting shares handed out to highly paid executives as "new stock issued."
analysis.who_benefits: The benefit to the general public is indirect: a higher tax makes buybacks somewhat more expensive, which nudges companies toward investing in plants, equipment, or workers instead, and it raises federal revenue that reduces deficits or funds other programs. Workers and communities that depend on corporate investment would benefit if firms responded by redirecting cash away from buybacks. Ordinary savers who hold stock only through index funds or retirement accounts would not benefit directly and could feel the cost as shareholders (see drawbacks).

how_it_helps.text: Quadruples the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, making it significantly more expensive for companies to funnel cash into buying back their own shares rather than productive investment.

Closes a bookkeeping loophole: under the existing 1% tax, a company can subtract the value of newly issued stock from its buyback total to lower its tax bill. The bill removes that subtraction for stock issued or given to 'covered employees' — the highly paid executives defined in the tax code — so companies can no longer offset buybacks with shares handed to top executives.
Applies immediately to repurchases after enactment, so companies could not stockpile buybacks in anticipation of the higher rate taking effect later.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock, and their shareholders, would pay the 4% excise tax directly. That includes large public companies that run large buyback programs — the biggest repurchasers are typically large-cap firms with large cash reserves — and, one step removed, investors in those companies, including retirement funds and index-fund holders. Executives whose stock compensation could no longer be used to reduce the tax would also bear some of the cost.

drawbacks.text: The tax is paid by corporations and their shareholders, and those shareholders include ordinary people's 401(k)s, pensions, and index funds — so some of the cost lands on ordinary savers rather than only on wealthy executives.

An excise tax on the transaction is a blunt instrument. A company determined to return cash to shareholders can switch to dividends (which are taxed differently) rather than change how it uses its profits, which would blunt any effect on investment while still collecting the tax.

Going from 1% to 4% may not be large enough to change corporate behavior much, in which case it would function mainly as a modest revenue raiser rather than a meaningful restraint on buybacks; the bill's sponsors did not provide an estimate of expected revenue in the summary or text.

By removing the adjustment for stock issued to covered employees, the bill narrows a general rule that allowed companies to net out stock issued for any reason; some companies issue new shares to fund employee compensation plans broadly, and the exception only distinguishes by whether the recipient is a highly paid executive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-targeted tax adjustment rather than a sweeping reform. The benefit to the public is real but diffuse — slightly more expensive buybacks, a closed loophole involving executive stock grants, and modest federal revenue — while the cost falls on identifiable public companies and their shareholders. The strongest honest objection is that the cost is shared by ordinary retirement savers who own stock indirectly, and that a 4% rate may be too small to change corporate behavior in a way workers would notice. On balance it would likely redirect a small amount of corporate cash and raise some revenue without major side effects, but it is also not a policy whose absence left most Americans measurably worse off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act of 2023 on February 14, 2023, joined by six original cosponsors: Senators Wyden, Schatz, Van Hollen, Reed, Luján, and Baldwin.
On the same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the standard first step for a tax bill.
The bill attracted a total of 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to the sponsor.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

key_actors.name: Sherrod Brown
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 14, 2023 and recruited 9 Democratic cosponsors, but the bill never advanced past referral in the Senate.

key_actors.name: Senate Committee on Finance
key_actors.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 14, 2023 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

key_actors.name: Ron Wyden and the original cosponsors (Schatz, Van Hollen, Reed, Luján, Baldwin)
key_actors.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill ultimately drew 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support.
